entry.title: Apache APISIX Under the Hood: The etcd-Driven Gateway Built for AI Traffic

link.title: Apache APISIX Under the Hood: The etcd-Driven Gateway Built for AI Traffic

entry.content:
Every serious AI stack hits the same wall eventually: model servers, vector databases, and agent backends all grow from a handful of services into a zoo of endpoints, each with its own auth scheme, its own rate limits, and its own idea of what a “normal” request looks like. Something has to sit in front of that zoo and make it presentable — terminating TLS, checking API keys, smoothing bursty traffic, and steering a /v1/chat/completions call to the right pool of GPUs. That something is an API gateway, and for inference-heavy workloads the gateway is not plumbing; it is the control surface for your entire serving budget.

Apache APISIX is an Apache Software Foundation gateway built on top of NGINX and etcd — its README says exactly that — with dynamic routing and hot-reloading of plugins as the headline features. It is written in Lua and runs inside OpenResty, the NGINX-plus-LuaJIT runtime, which means every request is handled by Lua functions woven directly into NGINX’s own request phases. Config is not baked into a config file at deploy time: the gateway watches etcd continuously, and route changes take effect within moments of an API call, with no reload and no dropped connections. Where Kong shares the same OpenResty foundation but traditionally keeps its source of truth in PostgreSQL, APISIX makes etcd the single source of truth and treats the data plane as a pure projection of it. If you read the earlier Traefik tour, you will notice the opposite philosophy again — Traefik is Go-native and provider-driven, while APISIX is C-adjacent, Lua-native, and store-driven.

The best way to understand a gateway like this is to trace one request through the source. This post walks the master branch of apache/apisix: how the worker boots, how routes are matched, how plugins are loaded and ordered, how upstreams are balanced, and where the Admin API fits in. Two diagrams anchor the tour — an overview first, then a deeper map — and every symbol referenced below was checked directly against the repository before being cited.

The APISIX surface at a glance: one CLI command boots OpenResty workers; the config store (etcd, or a local YAML file in standalone mode) feeds routes to the router; every request passes the access phase, the plugin framework, and the load balancer before reaching your upstream; the Admin API writes config back to etcd.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • CLI entry — start(), L1087 in the CLI turns apisix start into a rendered nginx.conf and a running OpenResty instance; the same module documents the stop and restart verbs around L178.
  • Worker bootstrap — http_init_worker(), L120 seeds randomness, starts the event bus, the LRU cache, timers, and then wires the config watcher, plugin framework, router, and Admin API handlers into the worker, one require(...).init_worker() per line through L172.
  • Config store — sync_data(), L722 in the etcd config module polls and watches etcd prefixes, while its counterpart sync_data(), L245 serves the same role for standalone-mode YAML files; which one is active is decided by core.lua, L34.
  • Router — router.lua, L81 builds the configured HTTP router; the default radixtree_uri match, L30 resolves one route per request using a radixtree keyed by URI, host, and vars.
  • Access phase — http_access_phase(), L915 is the per-request workhorse: it fetches a pooled api_ctx, matches the route, merges service and consumer configuration, and hands plugins their turn.
  • Plugin framework — plugin.load(), L420 requires every enabled plugin module once per worker; run_plugin(), L1362 then executes each plugin’s phase hook in priority order on every request.
  • Upstream and balancer — set_by_route(), L381 normalizes nodes, scheme, and TLS, after which pick_server(), L275 chooses a healthy node through the balancer module named by upstream.type (L154).
  • Admin API — run(), L176 dispatches REST calls on port 9180 to resource handlers like admin/routes.lua, L183, guarded by check_token(), L80.

The detailed map: request phases and the router on top, the plugin framework and a sample of built-in plugins in the middle, balancers and config providers below, with the Admin API closing the loop back into etcd.

From Install to Your First Model

The quickstart from the README is one command: curl -sL https://run.api7.ai/apisix/quickstart | sh. That script brings up APISIX listening on port 9080 together with its etcd configuration store. Confirm it is alive the README way: curl "http://127.0.0.1:9080" --head | grep Server — and watch for APISIX in the server header.

The first route is an Admin API call against port 9180:

curl -i "http://127.0.0.1:9180/apisix/admin/routes/1" -X PUT -d '
{
  "uri": "/get",
  "upstream": {
    "type": "roundrobin",
    "nodes": {
      "httpbin.org:80": 1
    }
  }
}'

A moment later, curl "http://127.0.0.1:9080/get" returns the httpbin response — the gateway proxied your first request without any reload. What happened under the hood is the part worth savoring: the Admin API validated the route schema in check_conf(), L54, wrote it into etcd, the etcd watcher picked up the change, and the router rebuilt its radixtree in each worker. None of that touched a config file.

From here the jump to model serving is exactly one more plugin. APISIX now advertises itself as an AI gateway, and the README lists the pieces: AI proxying to different LLM providers through a unified interface, load balancing with retries and fallbacks across multiple LLMs, token-based rate limiting to control cost, and security for AI workloads. In the source, that is the ai-* plugin family — ai-proxy, L56 rewrites a request into a provider’s API shape during the access phase and delegates to a provider module selected by conf.provider (L40), while ai-rate-limiting, L295 enforces token windows in the same phase. Because these are ordinary plugins with ordinary priorities, the same gateway that protects your /get demo also fronts your inference fleet, and pairing it with a Python backend built on FastAPI keeps the auth and throttling story in one place.

The Config Model: Watches, Not Reloads

The most distinctive design decision in APISIX is that nothing configures NGINX at request time — everything configures etcd, and the data plane follows. The etcd cluster holds every route, service, upstream, consumer, and plugin config as versioned keys. Each worker process runs a watcher for the prefixes it cares about: config_etcd.lua allocates a store per key with new(), L1053, starts its timers in init_worker(), L1256, and then loops in sync_data() fetching changed keys and firing an event per update. Consumers of a resource — the router, the plugin loader, the balancer — recompute their in-memory structures from those events.

This is why route changes propagate without downtime, and it is a genuinely different trade from gateways that re-render a config file and ask NGINX to reload. It is also why the standalone mode exists: config_yaml.lua implements the same resource interface on top of a local apisix.yaml file, polling its mtime in _automatic_fetch(), L421. The README calls this out as the friendly option under Kubernetes, where etcd’s operational overhead is a cost you did not ask for. The selection logic is a two-liner in core.lua, L24: read deployment.config_provider from the local conf, default to etcd, and require apisix.core.config_ plus that name.

One subtlety deserves emphasis: the Admin API and the data plane are peers, not master and minion. check_token() compares the X-API-Key header (or query argument or cookie) against the admin_key configured under deployment.admin; if you disable that check, you are trusting your network. The Admin API is served by the same OpenResty workers — http_admin() is just another phase hook — which keeps the deployment story to one binary plus one store.

Plugins: Lua Functions With a Priority Number

A plugin in APISIX is a Lua module that declares a name, a version, a priority, a JSON schema for its config, and hooks named after NGINX phases: rewrite, access, header_filter, body_filter, log. The framework sorts every plugin list by descending priority in sort_plugin(), L142 — higher numbers run first — and then calls only the hooks a phase needs. The numbers are a real routing decision: key-auth at priority 2500 runs its consumer lookup in rewrite, L110 before anything downstream sees the request; proxy-rewrite at 1008 mutates the upstream URI and headers in rewrite, L309; limit-req at 1001 shape-checks request rate in access, L138; prometheus at 500 collects metrics from its own api(), L105 endpoint instead of the request path.

The per-request glue is plugin.filter(), L575: given the matched route, it assembles the plugin list from route config, service config, and the authenticated consumer, so a single request can stack plugin configs from three levels. Merging happens before filtering — merge_service_route(), L763 folds service-level plugins into the route — and once a consumer is authenticated, consumer-level config can add plugins mid-request and even rerun the rewrite stage for the newcomers, which you can see at the bottom of the access phase around L1071.

The plugins directory holds well over a hundred modules, from jwt-auth to kafka-logger to the ai-* family, and the enabled list is itself config: plugin.load() reads it from the local conf at L421. In practice you enable a dozen, disable the rest, and pay only for the hooks you use — an execution model that keeps the Lua-per-request cost predictable.

Balancing Real Traffic

When the access phase finishes, handle_upstream() resolves the upstream: either an inline upstream object on the route, an upstream_id reference (including one chosen at runtime by the traffic-split plugin), or a domain that needs DNS resolution — see handle_upstream(), L716. set_by_route(), L381 then normalizes nodes into host-port-weight tuples, resolves scheme and TLS options, and fills in per-node details.

Node selection lives in pick_server(), L275. It consults active health checks, filters out unhealthy and warming-up nodes, and delegates to a picker module loaded dynamically by upstream type at L154: weighted round-robin in balancer/roundrobin.lua, L27, least-connections in balancer/least_conn.lua, L115, plus consistent hashing, EWMA, and priority-based pickers. After NGINX proxies the request, the balancer phase at http_balancer_phase(), L1662 can pick a different node on retry — for inference traffic, where one backend occasionally times out mid-generation, that retry path is the difference between a 502 page and a slow-but-successful answer.

Honest Limits

  • Two stores to operate. etcd is the heartbeat of APISIX, and it is a distributed system in its own right — quorum tuning, compaction, and backups are now part of your on-call rotation. Standalone YAML mode removes etcd but also removes hot config from remote sources.
  • Lua all the way down. The plugin model is a gift if you can write Lua, a chore if you cannot. WASM and external-plugin escapes exist, but the mainstream path is Lua on LuaJIT, and debugging a priority clash between twenty plugins is a skill you will build the hard way.
  • The Admin API is a control plane on the same box. Port 9180 is guarded by a single static API key from config, and it lives inside the same workers as the data plane. Front it with TLS and network policy, or it becomes the most interesting endpoint on the host.
  • Benchmarks are yours to run. The README makes no performance claims, and neither should you copy anyone else’s. The one number that matters is measured against your routes, your plugins, and your model servers.
  • The project moves fast. This tour reflects master at the time of writing; anchors can drift as the code evolves, which is exactly why every link in this post points at a pinned commit path you can re-check.

The verdict, in one line: if your traffic is API-shaped, bursty, and increasingly AI-shaped, APISIX is the rare gateway whose architecture — store-driven config, phase-native plugins, health-aware balancing — matches the problem rather than merely covering it. The source is approachable once you see the seams, and the two diagrams above are the map to keep open while you read it.

entry.title: Caddy: The Go Web Server Where HTTPS Is Not Your Job

link.title: Caddy: The Go Web Server Where HTTPS Is Not Your Job

entry.content:
Anyone who has put a machine learning model online knows the drill: you wrap a FastAPI app around your inference code, run it on port 8000, and then discover that the real work starts. Getting traffic to it over the public internet means a TLS certificate, a renewal process, an HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect, trusted proxy headers, and a reverse proxy config that quietly becomes the most fragile file you own. The same applies to Grafana dashboards, MinIO object storage, or any UI you bolt onto your ML stack. TLS termination is not glamorous, but it is the front door of every production AI system — and it is exactly the front door where misconfigurations turn into outages or leaks. We compared an alternative edge proxy in our Traefik deep dive, and Caddy takes a strikingly different stance on how that front door should behave.

Caddy is a web server written in Go whose headline feature is printed right at the top of its README: “Every site on HTTPS.” It was the first web server to use HTTPS automatically and by default, obtaining and renewing certificates from ACME authorities like Let’s Encrypt and ZeroSSL with zero configuration, and it manages a local certificate authority for internal names. Under the hood it is better described as an extensible server platform: a small config core plus “apps” (the tls and http apps ship standard), where every app, listener wrapper, matcher, and handler is a module. You can drive it with a friendly Caddyfile, with its native JSON config, or through a REST admin API — and all three converge on the same document.

This post walks through the source of caddyserver/caddy on the master branch with two diagrams and verified line anchors, so you can jump from picture to code. We will follow the life of a config from caddy run to a live listener, trace a request through matchers and the handler chain, and look closely at how automatic HTTPS is wired — including what Caddy does and does not promise.

Overview of Caddy's architecture: the CLI loads and adapts a config, the config core provisions apps, and the HTTP and TLS apps run listeners, routes, and certificate automation side by side.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • cmd.Main, L66 — the CLI entry point that parses OS arguments and dispatches the requested command, including caddy run defined in commands.go, L122.
  • cmdRun, L189 — the run command implementation: it sets resource limits, loads the config through LoadConfig, L107, then blocks while Caddy serves.
  • Adapter.Adapt, L32 — the Caddyfile adapter that lexes and parses your config text into Caddy’s native JSON document.
  • caddy.Load, L115 — the config runtime entry that applies JSON through changeConfig, skipping reloads when nothing actually changed.
  • App.Start, L481 — the HTTP app’s startup, which builds one http.Server per site block and binds every listener address.
  • Server.ServeHTTP, L598 — the per-request entry inside the http app: timeouts, access logging, HTTP/3 advertisement, and ACME challenge handling all happen here before user routes run.
  • RouteList.Compile, L239 — compiles the list of routes, each carrying a match and a handle list, into a single middleware stack.
  • Handler.ServeHTTP, L627 — the reverse_proxy handler, complete with a retry loop over upstream backends.
  • TLS.Start, L406 — the TLS app kicking off certificate management for all “automate” names, backed by the certmagic library that is pinned as a dependency in go.mod, L13.

The overview shows the county lines; the detail map below goes street by street, from the admin API’s localhost:2019 endpoint down to the matcher evaluation inside each route.

Detailed view: the CLI and Caddyfile adapter feed the config core; the admin API mutates the same config; the HTTP app binds listeners and runs the routing chain; the TLS app provisions certmagic policies and answers ACME challenges.

From Install to Your First Site

Caddy’s README is refreshingly blunt about installation: the simplest cross-platform path is to download a binary from GitHub Releases and place the executable in your PATH. If you want to build from source, you need Go 1.26.0 or newer, clone the repo, and build inside cmd/caddy; for plugins or version-stamped binaries there is xcaddy build. There is no runtime dependency chain — the README points out that Caddy runs anywhere with no external dependencies, not even libc.

The fastest possible serving session does not even need a config file. The file-server command is registered in fileserver/command.go, L40 with flags like --root, --listen, and --browse:

caddy file-server --listen :8080

That single line spins up a production-ready static file server on port 8080 — the same FileServer type used inside full configs, whose ServeHTTP lives at staticfiles.go, L329. For a long-running site you would write a Caddyfile instead. A minimal reverse proxy setup that forwards API traffic to a local model server looks like this:

example.com {
    reverse_proxy localhost:8000
}

Run it with caddy run --config Caddyfile. Two interesting things happen: first, cmdRun, L189 calls LoadConfig, which detects the Caddyfile and runs it through Adapter.Adapt, L32; if you are curious what JSON your Caddyfile produces, caddy adapt --config Caddyfile --pretty prints it (the command is defined in commands.go, L281). Second, caddy.Load, L115 applies that JSON, which cascades through changeConfig into run, L419: a context is provisioned, the admin endpoint is swapped in via replaceLocalAdminServer, L376, and every app’s Start is invoked in a loop with rollback if one fails (caddy.go, L444).

While serving, the same config document stays live. The admin API listens on localhost:2019 by default — the constant DefaultAdminListen is defined at admin.go, L1456 — and can POST a new JSON config or PATCH a fragment of it, with requests dispatched through unsyncedConfigAccess, L1181. This is why Caddy reloads never fork a new process: the config is data, swapped in place while listeners stay open.

Automatic HTTPS: certmagic Under the Hood

Automatic HTTPS is not a bolt-on module; it is a separate app that runs alongside the HTTP app. When the TLS app provisions (TLS.Provision, L166), it builds a certmagic certificate cache with a default capacity of 10,000 certificates. When it starts (TLS.Start, L406), it calls t.Manage on every name listed under tls automate, and certmagic — a separate library from the same author, pinned at v0.25.6 in go.mod — takes over issuance and renewal.

The automation rules themselves are declarative. AutomationConfig, L37 and AutomationPolicy, L91 describe which subjects get which issuers, and makeCertMagicConfig, L272 translates a policy into a certmagic config. By default Caddy uses ACME with both ZeroSSL and Let’s Encrypt as issuers (DefaultIssuers, L480), with multi-issuer fallback listed among README features, plus a fully-managed local CA for internal names like localhost.

One detail worth appreciating as a safety design: the HTTP-01 challenge has priority over your routes. Server.ServeHTTP, L598 guarantees ACME HTTP challenges by calling HandleHTTPChallenge, L810 before any user-defined handler chain runs — a stray route can never accidentally shadow your certificate renewals. This is the kind of guardrail you would otherwise have to remember to configure yourself with a hand-rolled proxy setup, and it is a large part of why serving a FastAPI inference app through our FastAPI tutorials behind Caddy “just works” on the TLS side.

The Request Path: Matchers, Routes, Handlers

Once a request arrives, the journey is deliberately boring — in the good sense. Server.serveHTTP, L847 performs hygiene first: it rejects over-long methods, enforces RFC 9112’s Host header requirements, and strips underscore/dot header aliases that could enable spoofing. Then the compiled primary chain runs at L950, wrapped by enforcementHandler, L963.

Routes are the heart of the http app. Each Route, L31 carries matcher sets under the JSON key match and handlers under handle; matcher sets are OR’ed while matchers inside a set are AND’ed. At request time wrapRoute, L256 evaluates the matchers — MatchHost.Match, L304 even uses a binary search fast path for large host lists — and, on a match, executes the route’s handler chain in middleware order. Handlers that produce a response (like file_server or reverse_proxy) belong at the end of a route, because the request flows down the chain and the response flows back up.

The reverse proxy handler deserves its own paragraph for the AI-serving use case. The Handler struct at L107 carries upstream pools, load balancing, health checks, transports, and a flush_interval that defaults to immediate flushing for streaming responses — exactly what you want when a language model is emitting tokens. proxyLoopIteration, L749 selects an upstream per attempt and drives retries, while roundTrip, L1639 performs the actual upstream round trip. If you deploy models with the Kubernetes recipes we published, this is the machinery answering your Service endpoints.

Running Caddy for Inference Endpoints

For an ML stack, a realistic Caddyfile fronts several services at once: an inference API, a dashboard, and maybe static model artifacts. Because routes are matcher-based, host and path dispatch live in one document, and the admin API means you can add a route with a curl call instead of restarting. Prometheus-style metrics scraping of your services also flows through the same listeners — see our Prometheus setup notes for the collector side.

Operations-wise, caddy start (defined at commandfuncs.go, L46 as cmdStart) launches Caddy in the background by spawning a child run process with a pingback confirmation handshake, so failed startups surface as errors instead of silent background deaths. Config survives restarts through an autosave file, and caddy reload swaps a new config into a running process over the admin API.

Honest Limits

Caddy’s automatic HTTPS depends on public reachability: ACME issuance requires that your domain resolves and that ports 80/443 are reachable, so it will not help inside air-gapped clusters — there you use the internal CA and accept untrusted roots, or bring your own certificates via certificate loaders. The code is also honest about on-demand TLS risk: TLS.Start, L406 logs a warning — “YOUR SERVER MAY BE VULNERABLE TO ABUSE” — when on-demand issuance is enabled without an ask endpoint or permission module, because otherwise any hostname hitting your server triggers a certificate request.

The Caddyfile, while delightful, is a projection of the JSON config, and README is explicit that JSON is the native language; some advanced configurations are only reachable in JSON, and adapters exist precisely because the Caddyfile cannot express everything. Placement of handlers also matters — the route compilation makes handler ordering meaningful, which is a learning curve if you come from an nginx-style include model. Finally, the trademark README insists the software is called “Caddy”, not “Caddy Server”, and the default admin endpoint binds to localhost:2019 only; exposing it to a network is a deliberate, opt-in decision you should make with an auth policy in mind. None of these are disqualifying — they are the edges of a design that leans hard on sensible defaults, and knowing the edges is what makes the defaults trustworthy.

entry.title: Contour: Reading the Go Source of the Envoy-Powered Ingress Controller

link.title: Contour: Reading the Go Source of the Envoy-Powered Ingress Controller

entry.content:
Every GPU cluster faces the same front-door problem. Model servers such as vLLM, Triton, or SGLang expose HTTP and gRPC endpoints, traffic has to shift gradually from one model version to the next, and the request flow must stay fast enough not to waste the GPUs sitting behind it. Contour is a Kubernetes ingress controller that answers it by deploying Envoy as a reverse proxy and load balancer, then translating the cluster’s routing intent — Ingress, the HTTPProxy CRD, and Gateway API — into Envoy configuration.

For AI/ML serving, that translation layer is the product. gRPC model servers need h2c pass-through, canary rollouts need weighted splitting between model versions, and long streaming completions need timeouts that do not cut off a slow generation. Contour encodes this as declarative objects, compiles them into an internal routing DAG, and streams the result to Envoy over xDS. Reading that compile step is the best way to understand what your ingress does with a request.

This post walks the main branch of projectcontour/contour as of 2026-11-02, from CLI entry point through DAG builders to the xDS gRPC server and metrics layer. Every symbol links to its real location, and both diagrams were generated from the same tour.

Contour's request flow: Kubernetes events are debounced, compiled into a DAG, translated into Envoy caches, and served to Envoy over gRPC.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main, L30 in cmd/contour/contour.go parses the CLI with kingpin and dispatches subcommands — serve, bootstrap, certgen, and the Gateway provisioner. Everything else on this page lives under serve.
  • Server.doServe, L388 is the wiring bench: it constructs the six Envoy resource caches at L503, the SnapshotHandler at L518, and starts the xDS server.
  • KubernetesCache.Insert, L124 in internal/dag/cache.go indexes every watched object — Services, Ingresses, HTTPProxies, Secrets — in memory, so rebuilds never re-hit the API server.
  • EventHandler.Start, L134 debounces the event storm behind a holdoff timer (100 ms default, 500 ms cap) before calling builder.Build() at L225 — one rebuild per burst, not per event.
  • Builder.Build, L59 runs the ordered Processor chain (defined at L29) and prunes invalid virtual hosts before returning the DAG.
  • HTTPProxyProcessor.Run, L127 is the heavyweight translator: it walks each HTTPProxy and produces virtual hosts, routes, and clusters, starting from computeHTTPProxy at L155.
  • SnapshotHandler.OnChange, L137 packages the resource caches into go-control-plane snapshots — the currency Envoy actually consumes.
  • xdsServer.Start, L904 waits for the initial DAG, then serves it: RegisterServer, L40 attaches all seven discovery services to one gRPC server.

Detail view: the three API dialects feeding the DAG processors, the resource caches, and the xDS serving path with metrics alongside.

The DAG: a Compile Step for Routing

The core design decision: Kubernetes objects never touch Envoy config directly. KubernetesCache (struct at L48) is the raw material, the DAG is the intermediate representation, and the Envoy resource caches are the output. Each processor gets a turn: GatewayAPIProcessor (L53) handles Gateway API objects, IngressProcessor (L34) handles core Ingress, HTTPProxyProcessor (L54) handles the CRD, and ListenerProcessor (L26) seeds one HTTP and one HTTPS listener for every distinct virtual host.

The output types read like a compiler’s AST: a Route at L307 holds match conditions plus weighted clusters, a VirtualHost groups routes under a hostname, and SecureVirtualHost adds TLS. Invalid configurations are recorded and pruned at the end of Builder.Build, so a broken include or missing certificate degrades to a clean 503 route instead of an inconsistent Envoy snapshot. If you know Kubernetes controllers, this whole-graph pattern will feel familiar: reconcile, prune, publish.

From Install to Your First Model

The quickstart in the repo’s own site is one command: kubectl apply -f https://projectcontour.io/quickstart/contour.yaml, which brings up Contour and Envoy in the projectcontour namespace. A Gateway provisioner path covers Gateway API setups, and contour bootstrap (wired at main L100, generating config via WriteBootstrap) serves hand-rolled Envoy.

With it running, a minimal HTTPProxy fronts a model server and canaries a new version — every field below checks out against the CRD types in apis/projectcontour/v1/httpproxy.go:

apiVersion: projectcontour.io/v1
kind: HTTPProxy
metadata:
  name: llm-router
  namespace: models
spec:
  virtualhost:
    fqdn: models.example.com
  routes:
    - conditions:
        - prefix: /v1/chat
      timeoutPolicy:
        idle: 300s
      services:
        - name: llm-v1
          port: 8000
          protocol: h2c
          weight: 90
        - name: llm-v2
          port: 8000
          protocol: h2c
          weight: 10

The semantics come straight from the type definitions: virtualhost makes the object a root proxy (HTTPProxySpec at L21), fqdn is required and regex-validated (L406), conditions and services are route fields (L643, L646), and weight (L1137) is documented as the percentage of traffic to balance. protocol: h2c comes from that field’s enum (h2, h2c, tls) and is what plain gRPC model servers want. Weighted entries like this are exactly how a 90/10 canary is expressed.

Serving xDS to Envoy

Envoy never polls Kubernetes; it holds open xDS streams and waits to be pushed state. Contour’s side of that contract lives in internal/xdscache/v3. The SnapshotHandler multiplexes two caches: a standard SnapshotCache for most resource types and a LinearCache for endpoints, because — as the comment at L49 explains — Envoy opens an EDS stream per CDS entry, and a naive cache would notify every stream on every endpoint change.

Endpoint traffic is high-volume, so it bypasses the DAG entirely. EndpointSliceTranslator (L292) converts EndpointSlice updates into ClusterLoadAssignments directly and triggers SnapshotHandler.Refresh (L96), while route and cluster changes ride the DAG path through RouteCache.OnChange (L62) and ClusterCache.OnChange (L68). On the serving side, request logging hooks in via NewRequestLoggingCallbacks, L29, and every Envoy node is hashed to a constant ID by ConstantHash, L26, so all replicas share one snapshot.

Metrics, Status, and the Event Layer

Metrics (L28) registers gauges for total, valid, invalid, and orphaned HTTPProxies plus a rebuild timer — Builder.Build wraps itself in prometheus.NewTimer at L75, so rebuild cost is directly visible in Prometheus. EventRecorder (L34) counts API-server events per operation before they reach the handler, and RebuildMetricsObserver (L63) re-derives route health counts after every rebuild.

Status flows back the other way. Processors write conditions into status.Cache (L60), and a StatusUpdateHandler flushes them to the API server. loadBalancerStatusWriter (L52) watches the Envoy Service and copies its assigned addresses into Ingress and Gateway status — the mechanism that makes kubectl get ingress show a real hostname instead of <pending>.

Honest Limits

  • Envoy is the only data plane. The README describes Contour as deploying Envoy as the reverse proxy; the code configures Envoy and never replaces it. If you want ingress and proxy in one binary, that is Traefik’s trade-off (see /traefik/).
  • xDS v3 only. The tree carries internal/xds/v3 and nothing else — there is no v2 fallback.
  • Rebuilds are whole-graph. Any meaningful change triggers a full builder.Build() after the holdoff (serve.go L611). Debouncing and the endpoint fast path mitigate this, but the rebuild is not incremental — the rebuild-timer metric exists precisely because that cost is real.
  • No performance claims here. The repo ships no benchmark numbers, so none are repeated; the README’s claims are limited to what Contour supports.

The lasting lesson for ML-serving infrastructure: treat ingress as a compilation problem — define intent as objects, compile to a graph, stream it to a data plane, and instrument every stage.
entry.summary: A source tour of projectcontour/contour: HTTPProxy CRDs, the internal routing DAG, xDS streaming to Envoy, and the metrics and status layer that watches it all.

entry.title: Envoy: Reading the C++ Source of the Cloud-Native Edge Proxy

link.title: Envoy: Reading the C++ Source of the Cloud-Native Edge Proxy

entry.content:
Ask anyone who runs LLM inference at scale who actually fronts their GPU fleet, and the answer is very often Envoy. The project — which describes itself on its README as a “cloud-native high-performance edge/middle/service proxy” — is the data plane underneath Istio, the default ingress for most Kubernetes stacks, and the load balancer sitting in front of many a vLLM or Triton deployment. Where our earlier tours of Traefik and Caddy followed Go codebases that read like web servers, Envoy is something else: a multi-million-line C++ engine whose every network hop passes through layered filter chains.

Why should an AI-infrastructure-minded reader care? Because inference workloads stress proxies in specific ways: long-lived gRPC streams for token-by-token streaming, request bodies that can be megabytes of prompt, sidecar meshes that need configuration to change without restarting pods, and aggressive retries that can turn one GPU outage into a thundering herd. Envoy was built for exactly these pressures, and its source code — the main branch of envoyproxy/envoy — is remarkably navigable once you know the load-bearing files.

In this post we read that source directly: the bootstrap entry, the listener manager that owns accept loops, the HTTP connection manager that turns bytes into streams, the cluster manager that dials upstream hosts, and the xDS control plane that reprograms all of it while running. We mapped the whole tour into two interactive diagrams; the overview below is the map, and the detail diagram later in the post zooms into each neighborhood.

Envoy at a glance: bootstrap code on the left, the server core, the listener fabric, the HTTP connection manager and router in the middle, the cluster manager dialing upstreams, and the xDS plus admin surfaces around them. Every box links to the exact source file.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main(), L16 — the binary entry point. It only does site-specific setup (including Windows service hosting) and hands control to MainCommonBase::run, L82, which switches between serve, validate and init-only modes.
  • InstanceBase::run, L1099 — the heart of the server. It builds a RunHelper (L1027) that waits for CDS initialization, then blocks in dispatcher_->run(...) — the main libevent loop.
  • InstanceBase::startWorkers, L982 — only after the cluster manager is ready does the server open the gates and start worker threads.
  • GrpcMuxImpl::genericHandleResponse, L342 — the xDS control plane. One multiplexed gRPC stream carries LDS, CDS, RDS, and friends; this handler routes each DiscoveryResponse to its watches. trySendDiscoveryRequests, L434 flushes the requests going the other way.
  • ListenerManagerImpl::startWorkers, L1392 — the listener manager hands its active listeners to every worker thread, one accept loop each.
  • TcpListenerImpl::onSocketEvent, L63 — the evented accept callback. Each accepted socket is wrapped and offered to the listener’s filter chain manager.
  • ConnectionManagerImpl::onData, L638 — the HTTP connection manager is itself just a network filter at the end of a chain. It feeds raw bytes to an HTTP codec, and newStream, L506 creates the per-request ActiveStream.
  • Router::Filter::decodeHeaders, L491 — the last HTTP filter for most traffic. It matches a route, resolves a cluster, and asks the cluster manager for a connection pool.
  • ClusterManagerImpl, L312 — the constructor of the object that owns every cluster, their thread-local host tables, and all pools; HostImplBase::createConnection, L685 is where a TCP dial actually happens.
  • AdminImpl::startHttpListener, L54 — a separate, tiny HTTP server on localhost for stats, config dumps and logging control.

The detailed view: bootstrap and server core at the top, listener fabric and workers on the left, the HTTP connection manager's decode/encode filter chains in the center, the router bridging to the cluster manager and host connections, with xDS subscriptions feeding configuration in from the side.

From Install to Your First Model

Envoy ships as a static binary; the fastest way to try it is the official image, envoyproxy/envoy on Docker Hub. Nothing about running it is Python-specific, which is exactly why it pairs well with Python model servers — the proxy terminates and routes traffic, the model server just speaks HTTP or gRPC.

admin:
  address:
    socket_address: { address: 0.0.0.0, port_value: 9901 }
static_resources:
  listeners:
  - name: listener_0
    address:
      socket_address: { address: 0.0.0.0, port_value: 10000 }
    filter_chains:
    - filters:
      - name: envoy.filters.network.http_connection_manager
        typed_config:
          "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.network.http_connection_manager.v3.HttpConnectionManager
          stat_prefix: llm_ingress
          route_config:
            name: local_route
            virtual_hosts:
            - name: gpu_backends
              domains: ["*"]
              routes:
              - match: { prefix: "/v1/chat/completions" }
                route:
                  timeout: 0s
                  cluster: gpu_pool
  clusters:
  - name: gpu_pool
    type: STATIC
    lb_policy: LEAST_REQUEST
    load_assignment:
      cluster_name: gpu_pool
      endpoints:
      - lb_endpoints:
        - endpoint: { address: { socket_address: { address: 127.0.0.1, port_value: 8000 } } }
        - endpoint: { address: { socket_address: { address: 127.0.0.1, port_value: 8001 } } }

The shape above follows the sample configs/envoyproxy_io_proxy.yaml checked into the repo, which uses the same two top-level keys: one admin listener and static_resources with listeners and clusters. Run it with the usual incantation, then poke the admin surface:

docker run --rm -p 10000:10000 -p 9901:9901 -v %cd%/envoy.yaml:/etc/envoy/envoy.yaml envoyproxy/envoy
curl http://localhost:9901/clusters

Two settings matter enormously for LLM backends. First, timeout: 0s on the chat-completions route — the default five-minute request timeout will happily kill a 4000-token streaming completion. Second, lb_policy: LEAST_REQUEST instead of round-robin: GPU latency is wildly variable per request, so sending the next prompt to whichever replica currently holds the fewest active streams is a much better default. The connection manager’s stream-level flow control (ActiveStream::decodeData, L1876) and the cluster manager’s pooling (ClusterEntry::httpConnPool, L1117) are what make per-request isolation real rather than aspirational.

The Listener Fabric: Workers, Accept Loops, Filter Chains

Envoy’s threading model explains most of its performance character. There is exactly one thread per worker, each with its own libevent dispatcher, and every listener is registered on every worker. The path from config to a listening socket is worth following in the detail diagram. Configuration arrives as a Listener proto and lands in ListenerManagerImpl::addOrUpdateListener, L608, which manages a three-generation dance (active, updating, draining) so that socket rebinding never drops in-flight connections.

Each listener becomes a ListenerImpl (L404), which resolves filter chains, socket options, and the transport sockets (TLS among them). When workers start, WorkerImpl::addListener, L73 posts the listener onto that worker’s own dispatcher — no locks on the hot path — and ConnectionHandlerImpl::addListener, L75 registers the active listener. On the worker thread, TcpListenerImpl::onSocketEvent, L63 fires per accepted socket, the connection handler matches it to a filter chain, and ListenerImpl::createListenerFilterChain, L1227 instantiates the actual network filters.

That last sentence is the key to Envoy’s design: at the network layer there is nothing special about HTTP. The HTTP connection manager is just the most famous network filter, and the same fabric carries TCP proxying, Redis, Mongo, or your own WASM extension. Once your head absorbs this — everything is a filter chain terminating in a terminal filter — the entire extensions tree stops being intimidating.

The Cluster Manager: Pools, Hosts, and the Data Path

The router filter is where request flow crosses from listener-land to upstream-land. Filter::decodeHeaders, L491 performs route resolution, then asks the thread-local cluster manager for a pool. The cluster manager is split into a global control-plane half and a per-worker thread-local half; the per-worker ClusterEntry::chooseHost (L2324) runs the load balancer — round-robin, least-request, ring hash, and so on — against a host table that updates without locks via ClusterEntry::updateHosts, L1667.

What makes this feel different from a typical reverse proxy is pooling. Envoy keeps per-host connection pools (HTTP/1, HTTP/2 multiplexed, HTTP/3) so that a burst of prompts to the same replica reuses warmed connections, including preconnection heuristics in ClusterManagerImpl::maybePreconnect, L1084. When responses come back, Filter::onUpstreamHeaders, L1941 is the retry and circuit-breaking decision point — this is where per-try timeouts, retries on reset, and idle-timeout handling live. For streaming inference, note that the response path (Filter::onUpstreamData, L2144) relays chunks immediately; there is no buffering step that would add latency between your tokenizer and the client.

xDS and the Admin Surface

Everything configurable in Envoy can arrive two ways: statically from the bootstrap YAML, or dynamically from a control plane. The dynamic half is xDS — a family of discovery protocols (LDS for listeners, CDS for clusters, RDS for routes, EDS for endpoint sets, SRDS, VHDS…) multiplexed over a gRPC stream. The subscription machinery starts at SubscriptionFactoryImpl::subscriptionFromConfigSource, L30, which turns a ConfigSource proto into either a file watcher or a gRPC subscription, and XdsManagerImpl::initialize, L137 wires the shared mux. Watches are registered in GrpcMuxImpl::addWatch, L136; responses flow through the handler we met in the overview.

The practical consequence for AI serving is hot reconfiguration. Adding a new model replica to EDS updates host tables on every worker without a socket blip. Draining a listener for a cert rotation happens through the same manager-generation machinery described above. This is the property that made Envoy the substrate for service meshes — and if you run on Kubernetes, you have almost certainly met it as an Istio sidecar, or via gateway products that embed the same engine; our earlier look at Traefik covers a Go-based alternative that trades some of this machinery for simplicity.

The admin surface is deliberately not a control plane. It is a localhost-only HTTP server (AdminImpl::startHttpListener, L54) with handlers registered via AdminImpl::addHandler, L522: /stats, /clusters, /config_dump, /server_info, plus runtime log-level changes. It is an operator’s stethoscope, not a CRUD API — the project is explicit that this interface has no authorization model and should never be exposed. For durable telemetry, export metrics to Prometheus — Envoy’s stats subsystem speaks that format natively — and trace spans to a collector such as Jaeger when you need to follow one slow completion across sidecars.

Honest Limits

  • No benchmarks from us. The README advertises the proxy as “high-performance” but ships no numbers, and we will not invent any. Envoy’s own performance measurement lives in the separate envoy-perf project, and results depend heavily on filter stack and hardware.
  • The build is heavy. This is a Bazel-driven C++ codebase of well over a million lines; a full build needs serious disk and time. If you want to modify it, plan for the Bazel toolchain, not a quick cargo build.
  • The v3 API is powerful but noisy. A minimal working config is fine; the moment you want mTLS, retry policies, and outlier detection, you are writing a lot of YAML or adopting a control plane to generate it.
  • Extension is C++ or WASM. There is no Lua-quick-edit story comparable to OpenResty-based proxies in-tree; Lua is available as a filter, but deep customization means recompiling or writing WASM filters.
  • Hot restart works, but it is a design you must respect. The parent/child restart protocol keeps uptime through upgrades, yet state that crosses generations has to flow through the documented handshake.
  • Self-description caveat: phrases like “cloud-native high-performance” are the project’s own marketing line, quoted here, not an independent measurement.

Even with those caveats, the codebase rewards reading. The same four objects — listener manager, connection manager, cluster manager, xDS mux — explain nearly every behavior you will observe in production, from a 503 during a mesh rollout to a mysteriously long first token after a config push. If GPU fleets, sidecars and streaming gRPC are part of your stack, an afternoon inside this source pays for itself many times over.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of Envoy's listener manager, HTTP connection manager, cluster manager and xDS control plane, with architecture diagrams.

entry.title: HAProxy: Reading the C Source of the Internet’s Favorite Load Balancer

link.title: HAProxy: Reading the C Source of the Internet’s Favorite Load Balancer

entry.content:
Every serious AI serving stack leans on a load balancer somewhere in front of its GPU fleet. Whether you are spreading traffic across four vLLM replicas, fronting an Ollama box with sticky sessions, or just keeping a FastAPI model server alive under bursty load, the software doing that work has to multiplex tens of thousands of sockets without falling over. HAProxy is the tool most of the industry reaches for, and it has earned that trust by being one of the most carefully engineered C programs in open source.

That engineering matters more in the AI era than it used to be. Model inference is an awkward workload for proxies: responses are long-lived, streaming, and token-by-token, so a connection that would have closed in 50 milliseconds for a webpage now stays open for 30 seconds while a large language model thinks. A load balancer that burns a thread per connection or wakes up on fixed timers will quietly eat CPU that your GPUs should be using. HAProxy’s answer is a single-threaded-per-core event loop that only wakes when something is actually ready — which is exactly the property you want between a busy frontend and an expensive inference backend.

So we cloned the repo, drew the architecture, and read the code. The diagrams below were generated from the actual source tree (the master branch, which at the time of writing is version 3.5-dev10 per the VERSION file). Every symbol link in this post points at a real function we verified in the tree. If you have read our takes on Envoy or Traefik, this is the C counterpart to those data-plane stories — older, stricter, and arguably still the performance reference point.

HAProxy at a glance: config parsing on the left, the per-thread event engine in the middle, and the accept-to-backend request flow on the right.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Startup and config. main, L3472 collects arguments and calls read_cfg, L1115, which loops over every config file and hands it to parse_cfg, L1384. Sections like frontend and backend are dispatched in cfg_parse_listen, L296.
  • Binding. After the config parses, protocol_bind_all, L316 opens every listening socket declared by the bind keyword.
  • The engine. run_thread_poll_loop, L3158 runs per-thread init hooks and drops into run_poll_loop, L3044 — the function that essentially is HAProxy at runtime.
  • Accepting. When a listener is readable, listener_accept, L1342 pulls client sockets, and the registered bind_conf->accept callback session_accept_fd, L218 builds the session and its first stream.
  • Proxying. The per-stream task process_stream, L1876 runs analyzers, and for upstream needs calls assign_server_and_queue, L978 followed by connect_server, L1811.
  • The mux. Byte-level HTTP lives in h1_process, L4269, which demultiplexes input into the internal HTX representation and serializes output.

The detail diagram zooms into those boxes, and the rest of this post walks through each layer with the same discipline: only claims we could point at in the tree.

The detailed view: config keyword parsers, the task and fd machinery under the event loop, the four balancer implementations, and stick-table storage.

The Event Loop Is the Whole Ballgame

If you only read one function in HAProxy, read run_poll_loop, L3044. It is about a hundred lines and it encodes the entire runtime philosophy. Each iteration it calls process_runnable_tasks, L714 to drain tasks that were woken since last time, then figures out how long it can afford to sleep, then hands control to the poller via cur_poller.poll at L3150. On Linux that poller is the epoll backend, whose _do_poll sits at ev_epoll.c L178. Sibling pollers for kqueue, poll, and select live in src/ev_kqueue.c, src/ev_poll.c, and src/ev_select.c, so the same loop runs everywhere; the mechanism changes, the shape does not.

Two details are worth savoring. First, the loop computes its sleep budget from the next timer expiry (next_timer_expiry) rather than waking on a fixed tick — an idle HAProxy with no traffic and no timeouts pending genuinely sleeps until the kernel has something to report. Second, when the poller returns, readiness is funneled through fd_update_events, L682, which marks file descriptors and wakes the tasklets that own them. From there run_tasks_from_lists, L486 executes tasks from per-class run queues under per-iteration budgets, which keeps one chatty connection from starving everyone else.

For an inference frontend this is exactly the behavior you want. Twenty concurrent streaming completions against a vLLM backend are just twenty quiescent sockets between tokens; the loop costs nothing while the model is computing. Compare that with the thread-per-connection cost model some simpler proxies still pay, or the shared-queue designs used by the ingress controllers behind Kubernetes fleets.

Listeners, Sessions, Streams

HAProxy’s vocabulary matters, so let’s define it the way the code does. A listener is a bound socket (listener_accept, L1342); when the backlog logic says the listener was throttled, dequeue_all_listeners, L756 brings it back later. A session wraps one accepted client connection — session_accept_fd, L218 allocates it via session_new, L75 and then runs frontend_accept, L50 for frontend-side setup like source checks and logging. A stream is one request/response exchange riding on that session, and its state machine is process_stream, L1876.

The split is deliberate and it is why multiplexing works: one HTTP/1.1 connection with keep-alive can host many streams over time, and the mux layer (h1_process, L4269, with h1_process_demux, L2220 parsing bytes and h1_process_mux, L3682 serializing output) is what converts raw socket events into the structured requests that analyzers in the stream layer consume. For GPU fleets this shows up as head-of-line sanity: each in-flight completion is a stream you can timeout, retry, or drain independently of the TCP connection it rides on.

Backends: Four Balancers and a Connection Game

Server selection happens in assign_server, L645, and the switch there is a museum of load-balancing algorithms, each in its own file: weighted round robin in fwrr_get_next_server, L562 (backed by ebtree structures), first-available in fas_get_next_server, L291, weighted least-connections in fwlc_get_next_server, L747, and consistent hashing in chash_get_next_server, L499, with static map-based hashing in map_get_server_hash, L262.

For model serving, the choice is not academic. Long, variable-duration inference requests make round robin misleading — a node can look fine while it holds ten 60-second streaming completions — so leastconn (fwlc_get_next_server, L747) is usually the sanest default for GPU backends. If your routing depends on which model a request targets (prompt cache locality!), consistent hashing via chash_get_next_server, L499 keeps the same model on the same replica more often than not.

After selection, connect_server, L1811 decides whether to reuse an idle connection or dial a new one through do_connect_server, L1447. Connection reuse is where a lot of real-world latency hides: TLS handshakes to a model server are expensive, and pooling is the difference between p99 being fine and p99 being sad.

Stick Tables: State Without a Database

The feature that sets HAProxy apart from most balancers is that it keeps per-client state in-process. A stick-table (parsed by proxy_parse_stick_table, L1916, registered among keywords at cfgparse-listen.c L3091) is created at parse time by stktable_init, L1195, and entries are stored and refreshed at runtime by __stktable_store, L718. Tables track counters — request rate, connection rate, bytes in — keyed by anything you can extract from a request, most commonly the source IP.

Why should an AI operator care? Because the cheapest defense of an expensive inference endpoint is a token bucket computed in the proxy. A tcp-request connection track-sc0 src rule (documented at configuration.txt L14918) plus a rate counter rejects scrapers before they ever reach the GPU queue — and every request you shed at the proxy is a full slot of batch capacity returned to paying users. Tables can even be replicated between nodes with the peers protocol (doc/peers.txt), which matters when you scale past one proxy box.

From Install to Your First Model

Enough archaeology — let’s stand one up in front of two inference replicas. Build from source per the INSTALL guide (or install a distro package), then write a config. Every keyword below is verifiable in doc/configuration.txt: balance at L6702, default_backend at L7949, server at L13179, and mode at L18571.

global
    log stdout format raw local0

defaults
    mode http
    log global
    timeout connect 5s
    timeout client  120s
    timeout server  120s

frontend llm_fe
    bind :8080
    default_backend llm_be

backend llm_be
    balance leastconn
    server gpu1 10.0.0.11:8000 check
    server gpu2 10.0.0.12:8000 check

Run it with haproxy -f haproxy.cfg -d (the -d flag keeps it in the foreground for debugging), point a client at port 8080, and watch requests round-robin — well, leastconn-spread — across your replicas. The check parameter turns on health checking so a crashed vLLM process is pulled from rotation automatically. If your model server speaks plain HTTP streaming (most FastAPI setups do), this config works as-is; the 120-second timeouts exist precisely because long completions must not be reaped mid-stream. Once it behaves, drop -d, daemonize, and you have a production-grade front door for less than a kilobyte of config.

Honest Limits

We verified every symbol link in this post against the tree, so here are the caveats with the same energy. First, we read master, and the VERSION file says 3.5-dev10 — this is a development branch, and HAProxy moves fast; function line numbers are accurate today and will drift. Second, any performance impression in this post is qualitative; the project’s own description (in the README) is “a free, very fast and reliable reverse-proxy,” and we deliberately did not invent benchmark numbers — measure against your own model-serving workload. Third, stick tables are bounded by the size you declare (per the stick-table syntax at configuration.txt L14461) and are per-node state; multi-proxy synchronization exists via the peers protocol but is a real operational decision, not a checkbox. Fourth, HAProxy is GPLv2-or-later per the README license note, which matters for some commercial embeds. Finally, the event engine is single-threaded per core with thread groups for scaling — massively parallel configurations are supported, but the mental model stays “one loop per core,” and NUMA-conscious deployment is on you.

Even with those limits, the takeaway stands: HAProxy is a small, readable core — an event loop, a config parser, four balancers, and a state table — that quietly fronts a very large fraction of the internet’s traffic. Reading it is a masterclass in doing more with less, and it is the baseline against which newer entrants in the same data-plane niche should be judged.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of HAProxy: the poll loop event engine, listeners and streams, balance algorithms, stick tables, and the config parser.

entry.title: ingress-nginx: Reading the Go Source of Kubernetes’ Most-Deployed Ingress Controller

link.title: ingress-nginx: Reading the Go Source of Kubernetes’ Most-Deployed Ingress Controller

entry.content:
Almost every Kubernetes cluster that serves an AI workload leans on an ingress controller at its front door, and for years the default door has been ingress-nginx: the reference NGINX-based controller maintained under the Kubernetes umbrella. When you expose a vLLM or Triton server behind a Service and route llm.example.com/v1 to it, this controller is very likely the component translating that Ingress object into a live nginx.conf. Its job sounds narrow — NGINX in, Kubernetes out — but the implementation is a fascinating piece of systems engineering: a configuration generator, a diff-and-reload sync flow, a validating admission webhook, and a leader election scheme, all in one Go binary.

The AI angle is not superficial. Streaming token output rides on long-lived HTTP responses and WebSockets, so the controller’s proxy timeout annotations matter more here than in a typical web app. gRPC model servers need HTTP/2 passthrough. Endpoint churn — pods rescheduled by an autoscaler in front of a GPU pool — hits the controller’s dynamic-endpoint path, which updates upstreams without restarting workers. Reading the source tells you exactly why your streaming responses time out and why a certain change triggers a full worker reload while another does not.

This post walks the repository at release v1.15.1 on the main branch. We generated two call-graph diagrams from the actual tree: a compact overview and a detailed map. Here is the overview.

Overview of ingress-nginx: the entrypoint builds the controller; the sync loop rebuilds the model from the store; OnUpdate renders and reloads nginx.conf; configureDynamically streams endpoint changes; leader election and the admission webhook sit on the side.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts at main, L53, which parses flags, builds the Kubernetes API client with exponential backoff, and checks cluster compatibility — the controller refuses to run on clusters older than v1.19 (main.go L104).
  • NewNGINXController, L76 wires the store, a rate-limited task queue bound to syncIngress (L145), the template writer, and the admission server into one struct, then Start, L272 brings them all up.
  • k8sStore.Run, L1239 starts informers for Ingress, Service, Secret, ConfigMap, EndpointSlice and IngressClass, maintaining a local cache so the sync loop never blocks on the API server.
  • setupLeaderElection, L45 contends for a Coordination Lease; only the leader publishes Ingress status.
  • syncIngress, L185 is the heart of the sync flow: it lists cached ingresses, builds the desired model via getConfiguration, L635, and hashes it to decide whether anything changed at all (L205).
  • When a change is real, OnUpdate, L680 renders nginx.conf through generateTemplate, L459, validates it with nginx -t, writes it, and issues nginx -s reload (L750).
  • After the reload, configureDynamically, L868 POSTs the endpoint tables as JSON to an embedded Lua endpoint so pod churn never forces a worker restart.
  • Finally, the admission webhook’s HandleAdmission, L54 screens every new Ingress before it can reach the sync loop at all.

The detailed diagram below expands each stage into the functions you would actually set breakpoints in, from the store informers to the status updater.

Detailed request flow map: store informers feed the task queue; syncIngress hashes the model and picks reload versus dynamic update; the render group turns TemplateConfig into nginx.conf; leader election and admission form two satellite groups.

The Configuration Generator: Ingress Objects to nginx.conf

ingress-nginx is, at its core, a template engine with strong opinions. The desired state is not a config file — it is a graph of Go structs. getConfiguration fans out into getBackendServers (controller.go L730), which walks every rule and path, and into createUpstreams (L1020) and createServers (L1269), which resolve Services to endpoints and hosts to server blocks. Annotations — the nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/* keys parsed by the extractor in internal/ingress/annotations — mutate these structs, which is why per-ingress behaviors like CORS, canary weights, or long read timeouts never appear in the Ingress YAML schema itself.

The data feeding this model is deliberately decoupled from the API server. Every watch — Ingress, Service, Secret, ConfigMap, IngressClass, and EndpointSlice for pod-level addresses — lands in the local store, and endpoint translation lives in a dedicated endpointslices.go inside the controller package. When an autoscaler adds a replica of your inference server, the EndpointSlice informer notices first; the store records the new address; only then does the sync loop recompute upstreams. This layering is also why the controller stays responsive on large clusters: nothing in the hot path waits on a network round trip to the API server.

The final struct is TemplateConfig (config.go L926), handed to a single Go template at rootfs/etc/nginx/template/nginx.tmpl. That template — thousands of lines — emits the http block (nginx.tmpl L62), one server block per host (L638), upstreams, and the TCP/UDP stream configuration. Before the result is trusted, testTemplate (nginx.go L644) runs nginx -t against a temp copy, so a broken render can never displace the running config.

The Sync Loop: Diff, Test, Reload

The event flow is deliberately boring, in the best way. Informers push events into the store; Start’s select loop (nginx.go L346) enqueues them; the queue coalesces bursts into one syncIngress call. The clever part is the diff. syncIngress fingerprints the desired configuration with a structure hash and compares it against the running one; if they match, it logs “no configuration change detected” and stops (L210). If they differ, IsDynamicConfigurationEnough (pkg/util/ingress/ingress.go L117) decides between two paths:

  1. Full reload — OnUpdate renders and swaps nginx.conf, then nginx -s reload starts new workers that drain old ones. This path is needed whenever server blocks, TLS certs, or most annotations change.
  2. Dynamic update — only endpoint tables changed, so configureDynamically PATCHes the Lua sidecar data inside NGINX with retries, and workers keep serving without interruption.

For GPU-backed model pools where endpoints scale in and out constantly, the second path is the reason latency does not spike on every autoscaler event. A health checker (checker.go L37) exposes /healthz and verifies that the dynamic load balancer has actually been initialized inside NGINX.

Two details make the loop production-grade. The queue is rate-limited — syncIngress begins by consulting a rate limiter (controller.go L186) — so a thundering herd of events cannot monopolize the single sync goroutine. And because nginx -s reload spawns fresh workers while old ones drain, the controller can optionally serialize reloads: with WorkerSerialReloads enabled, awaitWorkersReload (nginx.go L764) polls the worker count until it returns to the configured value before admitting the next reload. For clusters that churn configuration frequently, that option trades convergence speed for a predictable memory envelope.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation is one manifest. The official docs apply the provider bundle, which deploys the controller Deployment, Service, ServiceAccount, RBAC, and the validating webhook configuration in one shot:

kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/controller-v1.15.1/deploy/static/provider/cloud/deploy.yaml

That URL points at deploy/static/provider/cloud/deploy.yaml in this repository; bare-metal and AWS variants sit alongside it. Now assume your model server is a Service named vllm-svc on port 8000. A minimal Ingress that routes a host path to it looks like this:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: llm-api
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "3600"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: llm.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /v1
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: vllm-svc
            port:
              number: 8000

Every field here is resolved by the code we read: the controller selects the object because spec.ingressClassName matches its class (store.go L1068), pathType is validated and defaulted during the model build, and the service name and port feed createUpstreams. The proxy-read-timeout annotation is defined in internal/ingress/annotations/proxy (main.go L31) with the default nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io prefix (parser/main.go L33); the 3600-second value exists precisely so streaming LLM responses are not cut off mid-generation. Once the webhook approves the object and the sync loop fires, llm.example.com/v1 is live.

The image itself is worth a glance in the tree: the controller binary is built from cmd/nginx, while a second entrypoint at cmd/dataplane runs inside a chroot so that NGINX and the Go controller share a filesystem without granting NGINX workers a view of cluster credentials. Operators also get cmd/plugin, the source of the kubectl ingress-nginx plugin for inspecting backends, certs, and configs on a live deployment — handy when a model endpoint misbehaves and you want to see what the controller believes the upstreams are.

Leader Election and the Admission Webhook

Two satellite mechanisms keep the controller correct in replicas. First, setupLeaderElection wraps client-go’s elector around a Lease resource (status.go L104) named by the election ID, splitting the TTL into a renew deadline of half and a retry period of a quarter (L112). Only the leader starts the status syncer (internal/ingress/status/status.go L164), whose updateStatus (L273) copies the publish Service’s LoadBalancer addresses into every owned Ingress. Without election, three replicas would fight over status writes.

Second, the validating webhook intercepts Ingress create and update calls. ServeHTTP (internal/admission/controller/server.go L65) enforces a body-size cap, decodes the AdmissionReview, and hands it to HandleAdmission. The controller’s CheckIngress (controller.go L331) dry-runs the whole build: it filters the object into the cached set, extracts annotations, re-runs getConfiguration, and even renders the template (L438). Notably, the nginx -t subprocess inside admission is disabled — the code comments that it was deactivated to mitigate CVE-2025-1974 (L444), the “IngressNightmare” family of vulnerabilities where untrusted snippets could reach NGINX’s config language. Warnings such as deprecated annotations are attached via CheckWarning (L287) without blocking the request.

The status side is equally self-policing. The syncer computes which addresses to publish from the publish Service — runningAddresses (internal/ingress/status/status.go L183) — and can even detect that it is running as multiple pods (L239), publishing all of them so that client-side DNS round-robin mirrors reality. Addresses are standardized and deduplicated before any write, and the update is skipped when the resulting list compares equal to what is already recorded, sparing the API server from pointless writes on every resync.

Honest Limits

The project’s own README is blunt, and we adopt its claims rather than inventing our own. As of the announcement of November 2025, ingress-nginx is in retirement: best-effort maintenance runs until March 2026, after which there will be no further releases, bugfixes, or security patches, though existing deployments and artifacts remain available. The README explicitly advises new users not to adopt it and to look at Gateway API implementations instead — the Contour and Envoy ecosystems are the natural landing spots. The README also warns against multi-tenant production use, since anyone who can create Ingress objects is effectively a cluster administrator.

From the source, three further limitations are visible rather than advertised. Full-reload latency scales with configuration size, since every render re-emits and re-tests the entire nginx.conf. Snippet-style annotations, historically the escape hatch for arbitrary NGINX directives, are a security liability — the CVE fix above removed config testing from the admission path precisely because untrusted input reached that layer. And the controller requires Kubernetes v1.19 or newer, enforced at startup. If you are evaluating front doors for inference traffic, compare it with Traefik for its dynamic-config model, with our earlier Kubernetes internals tour for how Ingress fits the API machinery, and with the Gateway API generation of Contour and Envoy before committing.
entry.summary: A source tour of ingress-nginx: how the controller renders nginx.conf from Ingress objects, diffs and reloads, runs leader election, and gates traffic through its admission webhook.

entry.title: Istio: Reading the Go Source of the Service Mesh Control Plane

link.title: Istio: Reading the Go Source of the Service Mesh Control Plane

entry.content:
Serving large language models in production is rarely one process talking to one GPU. A realistic AI platform is a swarm of Kubernetes workloads: a tokenizer service, one or more vLLM or Triton replicas, an embedding server, a vector database, a gateway that fronts them all. Traffic between those pieces needs mutual TLS, weighted shifts when a new model version rolls out, retries when a replica OOMs mid-request, and latency metrics per route. That is exactly the problem a service mesh exists to solve, and Istio is the most widely deployed mesh for Kubernetes. This post is a source tour of the control plane — the istiod binary inside the istio/istio monorepo — read the way an engineer would read it: entry point first, then the machinery that turns a VirtualService YAML into Envoy configuration.

Why should an AI/ML infrastructure engineer care about Go source? Because every mesh feature you rely on at inference time is ultimately a loop of Go code: a controller notices your Deployment changed, a snapshot of services and policies is rebuilt, and a gRPC push streams new listeners and clusters to every Envoy sidecar near a model replica. When a canary rollout of a new model version behaves strangely — some pods still hit the old weights, one namespace did not get the policy — the explanation lives in this code, not in your Python. Reading it once pays off every time a mesh misbehaves at 2 a.m. while your GPU fleet is burning money.

The tour below follows master of istio/istio. I kept the graphs to two: a compact overview of the whole control plane, and a detailed map from Kubernetes watchers down to the generated Envoy protobufs, plus the sidecar injection path. Every code link points at a symbol I actually located and read in the tree, with its line number.

Istio control plane at a glance: one istiod binary, one aggregated registry, one xDS server feeding every Envoy, and a webhook that adds sidecars at pod admission.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main, L27 is the whole entry point of pilot-discovery — it builds the root cobra command and executes it. Almost everything else in the control plane hangs off this call.
  • NewServer, L234 in pilot/pkg/bootstrap assembles the control plane: it creates the model Environment, wires the aggregated service registry, starts config controllers, and only then opens the xDS gRPC listener.
  • aggregate.Controller, L40 fuses several registries (Kubernetes clusters, ServiceEntry sources) into one view; the kube.Controller, L195 watches Services and EndpointSlices in each cluster it is attached to.
  • crdclient.Client, L58 is how Istio CRDs — VirtualService, DestinationRule, and friends — become uniform config.Config records flowing into the mesh model.
  • DiscoveryServer, L90 is the gRPC xDS server. Its Push, L317 method debounces updates, rebuilds the push context, and fans out to every connected proxy.
  • InitGenerators, L29 fills the generator map — CDS, LDS, RDS, EDS generators that wrap the ConfigGeneratorImpl, L56, the single place where the mesh model is translated into Envoy resources.
  • RunTemplate, L449 is the sidecar injection core: the webhook merges the Envoy proxy template into your pod spec at admission time, before any container starts.

The detailed map: Kubernetes watchers and CRD clients on the left, the PushContext snapshot in the middle, per-type xDS generators and the Envoy config synthesizer on the right, with the injection webhook hanging off bootstrap.

Pilot’s Job: One Registry, Thousands of Proxies

Istio’s control plane used to be three separate binaries; today it is one, istiod, and the source lives under pilot/. The naming still betrays the history: pilot-discovery is the main command, and its main, L27 is deliberately boring — enable klog, build the root command, execute. The interesting work starts in NewServer, L234, which reads like a table of contents for the rest of the codebase. Line 238 constructs the aggregate.Controller, L40, line 270 constructs the xDS DiscoveryServer, L90, and line 271 wraps it with a NewConfigGenerator that owns an xDS response cache.

The registry side answers a simple question with a lot of machinery: which services exist, and where do their endpoints live? For a Kubernetes cluster, kube.Controller, L195 runs informers over Services, Pods, and EndpointSlices; the EndpointSlice tracking code converts each slice into Istio’s internal endpoint shards, keyed by service and cluster. Those shards are what EDS will later serialize for Envoy. Multicluster setups simply add more registries to the aggregate — the mesh model never sees more than one logical view.

Configuration follows the same shape. initConfigController, L79 builds a store whose Kubernetes implementation is the crdclient.Client, L58. Everything Istio accepts — VirtualService, DestinationRule, Gateway, Sidecar — is normalized into config.Config, a flat struct of type, name, namespace, and spec. That normalization is why the rest of Pilot can be agnostic about where a piece of config came from.

Inside the xDS Machine Room

When a sidecar connects, StreamAggregatedResources, L184 registers the connection and enters a loop that processes discovery requests. When the mesh changes instead, ConfigUpdate, L359 submits a push request into a debounce channel. Push, L317 then does two things that matter for anyone operating an AI platform: it rebuilds a fresh PushContext, L205 — a coherent snapshot where InitContext, L1359 has already indexed services, endpoint shards, and policy defaults — and then hands the snapshot to every generator. The pending proxies go through a PushQueue, L23 so slow or overloaded proxies cannot stall the rest.

The type-URL dispatch is tidy. findGenerator, L73 looks up which generator owns a type, and pushXds, L112 calls it and ships the resources. The generator map is filled once by InitGenerators, L29: the EdsGenerator, L95 for endpoints, CdsGenerator.Generate, L137 for clusters, LdsGenerator.Generate, L120 for listeners, RdsGenerator.Generate, L104 for routes. Delta xDS, the incremental flavor that saves bandwidth on big meshes, enters through StreamDeltas, L44 and converges on the same generators.

The actual Envoy shapes are produced under pilot/pkg/networking/core. BuildClusters, L64 expands each Service, L77 into Envoy clusters — one per subset, per port, honoring load-balancing and TLS settings. BuildListeners, L118 builds the inbound and outbound listener tree, filtered through the proxy’s SidecarScope, L154 so a namespace-limited proxy only learns its slice of the mesh. This is the mechanism that makes mTLS between your tokenizer and your LLM server “just work”: the listener and cluster builders insert the correct transport socket from PeerAuthentication and DestinationRule state, and Envoy enforces it on the wire.

VirtualService, DestinationRule, and the Mesh Model

VirtualService is the API an ML platform touches most. A routing rule like “send 10 percent of /predict traffic to the new quantized model” is a VirtualService; the code path that consumes it is BuildHTTPRoutes, L56, which walks the proxy’s visible VirtualServices and delegates each one to BuildHTTPRoutesForVirtualService, L393. Per-rule conversion happens in TranslateRoute, L514, which turns match blocks, weighted destinations, retries, mirrors, and header rewrites into Envoy route protos.

DestinationRule supplies the subsets those destinations refer to. Pilot merges port-level, subset-level, and top-level traffic policies in ConvertConsolidatedDestRule, L259 — worth knowing when you wonder why a connection-pool setting at the subset level shadowed your mesh-level one. The push context also computes VirtualService-derived state up front in initVirtualServices, L1783, including hostname conflict detection, so two VirtualServices claiming the same host fail loudly at push time rather than silently at Envoy.

Two AI-specific notes. First, Istio’s Gateway API implementation under pilot/pkg/config/kube/gateway/ includes first-class handling of the Kubernetes Inference Extension — the InferencePool collection tracks pools of model-server endpoints that a Gateway can load-balance across, which is the standards-track way to route to a pool of LLM replicas. Second, telemetry: the same sidecars that route traffic export metrics for Prometheus and traces for Jaeger, so per-model latency percentiles fall out of the mesh without instrumenting your inference server.

Sidecar Injection: The Webhook That Ships Envoy

Nothing in a pod asks for a proxy; the cluster asks for the pod. When you label a namespace for injection, istiod’s mutating admission webhook intercepts pod creation. The wiring starts at initSidecarInjector, L43, which loads the injection template from the istiod configmap, and the HTTPS server that receives AdmissionReviews comes from initSecureWebhookServer, L47. The merge itself is RunTemplate, L449 in pkg/kube/inject: it takes the admission request, overlays values from the namespace and pod annotations, and rewrites the pod spec with the istio-proxy container, the istio-init setup, and the workload identity plumbing. The Webhook, L112 struct tracks the template and values it needs. The per-pod companion is the agent binary, pilot-agent, which starts Envoy with a bootstrap config and then proxies xDS to it.
