For an inference fleet this means every model pod gets its Envoy for free at scheduling time — and gets a SPIFFE workload identity that mTLS is built on. Rotate the mesh CA, and every sidecar picks up a new cert; retire an old model version, and its sidecars simply stop receiving traffic once the VirtualService weights move.

From Install to Your First Model

Getting a mesh onto a cluster is one binary’s job: istioctl install. The CLI’s install command is implemented in the operator tree at InstallCmd, L137, which renders the IstioOperator spec into manifests (the operator/cmd/mesh package also backs istioctl manifest generate) and applies them. A minimal profile is enough for a dev cluster:

istioctl install --set profile=minimal -y
kubectl create namespace llm-serving
kubectl label namespace llm-serving istio-injection=enabled

With injection enabled, deploy your model server as usual — a Deployment running vLLM behind a Kubernetes Service. Once the pod comes up with two containers (llm-server and istio-proxy), you can already route with mTLS. The first VirtualService worth writing is a canary: send 90 percent of traffic to the current model and 10 percent to a fine-tuned candidate, using the same shape Istio’s own bookinfo sample uses for its reviews service (see samples/bookinfo/networking/virtual-service-all-v1.yaml in the repo):

apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: llm-inference
spec:
  hosts:
  - llm-server
  http:
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: llm-server
        subset: vllm-stable
      weight: 90
    - destination:
        host: llm-server
        subset: vllm-candidate
      weight: 10

The subsets come from a matching DestinationRule with version labels. Apply both, and within a push cycle the Envoy sidecars in front of your clients hold new route tables with the weighted split — no restarts, no ingress changes. istioctl analyze will flag missing DestinationRules or conflicting hosts before you apply, which is cheaper than discovering them in production.

Honest Limits

Claims in this section are either from the repository itself or attributed. The README describes Istio’s parts as Envoy sidecars, the Rust ztunnel proxy for ambient mode, and istiod providing “service discovery, configuration and certificate management” — that is the control plane we toured, and it is the accurate summary of scope; istiod does not do data-plane forwarding itself. The two diagrams above were generated from the actual master tree, but the repo is enormous — my indexed subset of just four top-level directories (pilot, istioctl, pkg, operator) already spans thousands of files, so treat the graphs as a map of the control-plane core, not the whole project: the CNI plugin, ambient ztunnel (a separate Rust codebase), and the CA code paths are deliberately out of frame.

I verified every symbol link in this post at its stated line on master at the time of writing; the line numbers will drift as the project moves, and if a symbol has moved by the time you read this, searching the function name in the linked file’s package is the reliable recovery. Finally, nothing here is a performance claim: how much proxy overhead your inference traffic tolerates depends on request patterns, mesh size, and hardware, and the project’s own benchmarks — not this post — are the place to look for numbers.
entry.summary: A guided tour of istiod in the istio/istio repository: xDS generation for Envoy, VirtualService and DestinationRule processing, sidecar injection, and what all of it means for AI inference fleets.

entry.title: Inside Kong: The Lua Gateway That Wraps Nginx into an AI Traffic Machine

link.title: Inside Kong: The Lua Gateway That Wraps Nginx into an AI Traffic Machine

entry.content:
If you have ever served a machine-learning model to real users, you have run into the same trio of problems: you need to throttle who can call your inference endpoint, authenticate those calls, and decide which model version a request should hit. A raw FastAPI app can do all three, but then every team reimplements rate limiting, API keys, and per-tenant quotas in application code. That is exactly the gap an API gateway fills — a reverse proxy with policy. And when the “service” behind the gateway is an LLM rather than a CRUD API, the policy surface grows: token budgets, prompt filtering, per-provider routing, caching. Modern gateways have been retrofitted for that world, and Kong is one of the most complete examples.

Kong (the open-source Kong Gateway from Kong Inc.) is a cloud-native, platform-agnostic API, LLM, and MCP gateway whose distinguishing engineering decision is old and clever: it is a set of Lua modules running inside OpenResty, which means inside Nginx itself. There is no sidecar rewriting your traffic between processes. Each incoming request is handled by Nginx’s event loop, and at defined points of that loop Kong invokes your Lua plugins through a Plugin Development Kit — a global kong table that plugins use to read the request, mutate headers, call the upstream, and short-circuit responses. The entire core is in kong/, a directory of plain Lua files.

That architecture gives you a rare property for debugging: the gateway’s behavior is legible from a handful of files. In this tour we read Kong at master (v3.10.0, kong/meta.lua) and follow one request from the nginx config template through routing, plugin execution, load balancing, and out to the upstream. If you are comparing gateways, we have done similar tours of Traefik and Caddy — both Go-native, both built on different assumptions than Kong’s.

Overview: bootstrap loads kong.conf and builds the global kong PDK; the generated nginx config wires the runloop phases; each request flows through the router, the plugins iterator, and the balancer, all backed by the DAO layer, with the Admin API controlling it all on port 8001.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Bootstrap — the entry file plants the global PDK table: _G.kong = kong_global.new(), L65, then require "kong.db", L68 and require "kong.runloop.handler", L71 pull in the data and request layers.
  • Config — conf.loaded_plugins, L839 is where plugins = bundled in kong.conf gets merged with the bundled plugin map, deciding what this node can run.
  • Ports — defaults live in proxy_listen ... 0.0.0.0:8000, L27 (traffic), admin_listen = 127.0.0.1:8001, L29 (control), and Kong Manager on admin_gui_listen = 0.0.0.0:8002, L30.
  • Nginx wiring — the templated server block binds phases to Lua: rewrite_by_lua_block { Kong.rewrite() }, L145, access at L149, header filter at L153, and the upstream with proxy_pass $upstream_scheme://kong_upstream$upstream_uri, L216.
  • Per-request runloop — access = {, L1184 is the heart: it matches the route, then prepares and executes the balancer.
  • Routing — the router factory FLAVOR_TO_MODULE, L17 selects the matching engine: the default traditional flavor, or expressions.
  • Plugins — kong.db.plugins:each, L523 pages configured plugin entities out of the DAO layer to build the per-request iterator.
  • Data layer — entity schemas are validated and DAOs attached in one place: daos[schema.name] = DAO.new(...), L115.
  • Control plane — the Admin API auto-generates CRUD endpoints for every entity schema at routes = Endpoints.new(dao.schema, routes), L93.

Detail: the bootstrap/CLI, the PDK namespaces, the generated nginx template, the runloop (handler, plugins iterator, balancer), the three router flavors, the DAO/strategy layer, the Admin API app, and four bundled plugins with their execution priorities.

Why an OpenResty Foundation Matters

Most gateways you would compare Kong against — Traefik in Go, Envoy in C++ — run their own event loop. Kong instead extends Nginx’s. The generated nginx-kong.conf is a real nginx configuration where every phase hook is a Lua callback: the template around rewrite_by_lua_block, L145 is rendered by Kong itself, so the gateway you run is literally an nginx.conf with Lua islands in it. This means TLS termination, access logs, upstream keepalive, worker tuning — all nginx, battle-tested, zero new code. Kong adds balancer_by_lua_block at L85 to make the upstream dynamic: instead of a static server list, a callback chooses the target at connection time.

The cost of this design is equally real: plugins execute inside Nginx worker processes in Lua, so a blocking call in a plugin stalls the whole worker. Kong’s PDK is deliberately non-blocking for I/O (it uses cosockets), and plugin authors must respect that contract. It is a different engineering culture than Go gateways, closer to how OpenResty communities have always built.

The Request-Phase Machine

Kong’s mental model is a sequence of nginx phases, and each request walks them. Kong.rewrite() (registered at function Kong.rewrite(), L1112) runs first for HTTP; for stream subsystem traffic there is a preread phase that inspects TLS handshakes. Then Kong.access() — defined at function Kong.access(), L1186 — does the heavy lifting: runloop.access.before(ctx), L1205 matches the Route, then the plugin iterator runs, then runloop.access.after(ctx), L1240 finalizes the upstream decision. If nothing matches, the request dies there with kong.response.error(404, "no Route matched with those values"), L1225.

The plugin execution machinery is the subtle part. During the rewrite phase, Kong does a single pass over the configured plugins with execute_collecting_plugins_iterator (defined at L367); each plugin’s later-phase handlers — access, header filter, body filter, log — are collected into the request context then, so the per-phase loops later are just replaying that list. The invocation itself is a coroutine per plugin: coroutine.create(plugin.handler[phase]), L399. The coroutine boundary is what makes “delayed response” work — a plugin can, for example, produce its own response and stop proxying without raising an exception.

The PDK that plugins call is the global kong table. kong_global.init_pdk at L161 injects PDK.new(kong_config, self), which instantiates every module from MAJOR_MODULES at L193: kong.request, kong.response, kong.service, kong.table, kong.log, kong.vault, kong.tracing, and friends. Phase guards are enforced at runtime with bitmasks from rewrite = 0x00000010, L15 — call kong.response.exit in the wrong phase and you get a loud error rather than silent misbehavior.

Plugins: Priorities, Combos, and the AI Families

A Kong plugin is a Lua module with a PRIORITY number and per-phase handler methods. Ordering falls out of those priorities: key authentication runs first at PRIORITY = 1250, L22, rate limiting after it at PRIORITY = 910, L57, and the AI plugin family further down. Configuration lookup happens per request through “combos” — the iterator resolves the most specific of global, service-level, route-level, and consumer-level configs (the lookup chain lives in plugins_iterator.lua’s lookup_cfg).

The interesting 2024–2026 addition is the AI family. kong/llm/ contains adapters and drivers, and the ai-proxy plugin (priority 770, L4) rewrites a request to any major LLM provider — OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Gemini — behind one route. Companions like ai-prompt-guard police what prompts may contain. In practice this turns the gateway into a universal LLM endpoint: clients speak one schema, Kong handles provider dialects, credentials stay out of application code, and rate limiting/token tracking apply uniformly. That is the same value proposition gateways gave REST APIs a decade ago, applied to inference — which is also why pairing Kong with a gateway-agnostic SDK such as LiteLLM works so well: one layer owns transport policy, the other owns model abstraction.

From Install to Your First Model

The repository README keeps installation honest and boring: the fastest verified path is the docker-compose distribution — clone Kong/docker-kong, then KONG_DATABASE=postgres docker-compose --profile database up. Once the stack is up, the README confirms the ports you saw in kong_defaults.lua: :8000 for proxied traffic, :8001 for the Admin API, :8002 for Kong Manager. From source, the same things happen via the CLI: kong start is implemented in kong/cmd/start.lua (execute at L46), which loads configuration, runs migrations, renders the nginx template, and signals Nginx to launch workers.

To proxy an LLM inference API you then do the REST dance against :8001: create a Service whose url points at, say, your internal model server; create a Route under it with a path prefix; attach key-auth and rate-limiting plugins (a POST per plugin with JSON config). Add ai-proxy in front of an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and your clients now hit Kong on :8000 with your API keys, not the provider’s. Every one of those operations is the Admin API app at kong/api/init.lua dispatching through the generated endpoints into the DAO layer — and because entities are defined in CORE_ENTITIES at L136 (services, routes, consumers, plugins…), the CRUD surface for each was derived from its schema, not hand-written. For metrics, point Prometheus at the prometheus plugin’s endpoint, and for k8s deployments the ingress controller wraps the same gateway.

Router, Balancer, and the Data Layer

Route matching has three flavors selected by the factory at FLAVOR_TO_MODULE, L17: traditional (method/host/path/headers with prefix and wildcard semantics), expressions, and traditional_compatible. The expressions flavor is backed by an ATC (any-tree-of-comparisons) engine in kong/router/atc.lua — you write matching rules as small boolean expressions instead of field-by-field config. Once a Route matches, the runloop builds balancer_data and calls balancer.execute(balancer_data, ctx), L290, which dispatches through algorithm modules (round-robin, least-connections, consistent-hashing, latency-based) and integrates active/passive health checks. Retries on a failing target ride nginx’s proxy_next_upstream machinery via upstream_retry.lua, invoked from the generated config.

The data layer is a small ORM. kong/db/init.lua validates each entity schema against a metaschema at L62 and attaches a strategy: PostgreSQL, or off for DB-less mode where a declarative YAML/JSON file is the database (parsed in kong/db/declarative/init.lua). DB-less matters for GitOps and edge cases — the whole gateway state ships as one config file. Between the control plane and data plane there is also a cache tier (kong/cache/) so workers do not hit Postgres on every request; that is why you can change a route via :8001 and see workers pick it up by polling a cache version key rather than reloading.

Honest Limits

  • Lua is the price of admission. Writing or debugging a custom plugin means Lua, and the single-threaded-per-worker model means one blocking call in plugin code stalls other requests on that worker. Go and Python external plugins exist (the plugin server machinery lives in kong/runloop/plugin_servers/), but the first-class experience is Lua.
  • Two components, not one. With the Postgres strategy you operate a database; with DB-less you take on declarative-config workflows. Either way the Admin API is an attack surface to lock down — it binds to 127.0.0.1:8001 by default for good reason.
  • Feature surface vs. license. The repo is Apache-2.0, but several enterprise capabilities (RBAC, some AI features, advanced analytics) live in Kong Enterprise or Konnect, not in this source tree. Reading the code tells you what community Kong actually does, which is less than the marketing pages suggest and more than enough for the core proxy job.
  • The modern alternative lanes. If you only need gateway features in-process, FastAPI middleware may be enough; if you want a config-first Go binary, Traefik or Caddy; if you need L2/L4 muscle, Envoy. Kong’s sweet spot is many teams, many services, one policy point — the situation where a gateway pays for itself.
  • AI gateway features move fast. The kong/llm/ layer and AI plugins churn between releases; check the changelog before betting on specifics.

Kong’s source rewards the read because it has one clear idea — nginx phases + Lua coroutines — executed consistently across thousands of files. Once the phase machine clicks, the router, balancer, and DAOs all feel like consequences rather than surprises.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of Kong Gateway — OpenResty internals, the request-phase model, Lua plugins, and how the same code path proxies both REST APIs and LLM traffic.

entry.title: Linkerd: Reading the Rust and Go Source of the Lightest Service Mesh

link.title: Linkerd: Reading the Rust and Go Source of the Lightest Service Mesh

entry.content:
Modern AI inference is quietly becoming a distributed-systems problem. A production stack today is rarely one container: there is a gateway, a tokenizer, a prefill-versus-decode split across GPU pods, a vector database, maybe a reranker, and a scrape target for metrics. Every hop that crosses a pod boundary is a place where a stray connection, an unauthenticated client, or a stalled upstream hurts tail latency. Linkerd positions itself exactly at those boundaries. Its README calls it “an ultralight, security-first service mesh for Kubernetes” that adds “critical security, observability, and reliability features to your Kubernetes stack with no code change required” (README.md, L13). For clusters serving models, the pitch is concrete: mTLS between the gateway and the inference service, retries and timeouts without touching Python, and per-route telemetry, all applied by a proxy that sits next to the GPU pod rather than inside it.

What makes Linkerd interesting to read is that it is not one language but two, split deliberately. The linkerd2 repository holds the control plane: the destination and identity services, the proxy injector, and the CLI are Go, while the policy controller — the brain that decides which clients may talk to which ports — is a set of Rust crates. Compared with Envoy-based meshes such as Istio, Linkerd’s sidecar is written in Rust and developed in a separate repository, which keeps this codebase small enough to actually tour in an afternoon. If you have read our Kubernetes source tour, many building blocks here will look familiar: informers, admission webhooks, and gRPC streaming everywhere.

This post tours the linkerd/linkerd2 repository as it exists on main, and the diagrams below were generated directly from the source tree. Two things up front, in the interest of honesty: the data-plane proxy itself is not in this repo (more in the limits section), and every code link below points at a symbol I verified by reading the source, not by paraphrasing a blog post.

Overview: the CLI and injector put a Rust sidecar into every pod; the Go control plane serves addresses, profiles, and certificates; the Rust policy controller watches Kubernetes objects and answers policy queries from the proxy.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • newCmdInstall, L89 renders the control-plane Helm charts through the embedded Helm engine, so linkerd install emits plain Kubernetes manifests.
  • Inject, L31 is the admission handler that mutates pods annotated with linkerd.io/inject at deploy time.
  • GetPodPatch, L770 builds the JSON patch that adds proxy-init and the sidecar container to a workload.
  • NewServer, L87 assembles the destination service, the gRPC API the proxy calls for every destination it wants to reach.
  • NewEndpointsWatcher, L83 tracks Services, Endpoints, and EndpointSlices so the destination service can stream live address sets.
  • NewService, L174 constructs the identity service whose Certify, L212 gRPC method signs workload certificates.
  • Index, L53 is the Rust policy index linking Pod ports to Server and ServerAuthorization resources.
  • InboundPolicyServer, L29 implements the policy gRPC API that the proxy consults before admitting a connection.
  • linkerd2-proxy, L26 — the proxy consuming all of the above — is listed in the README as a separate repository.

Detail view: the injection path (CLI and webhook share one library), the destination and identity services, and the Rust policy crates from k8s index through gRPC servers, with the proxy as the external consumer of all three APIs.

The Policy Controller: One Index for Every Port

The most self-contained story in the repo is the policy controller, a Rust workspace under policy-controller/. Its crate documentation states the data model plainly: each Pod enumerates its ports, each Server selects pods in the same namespace, and each ServerAuthorization selects Server instances (lib.rs, L6). The index that maintains these links is Index, L53, and when the gRPC layer asks about a specific pod and port, pod_server_rx, L202 hands back a watch receiver for that port’s current policy. It is a cache-first design: the controller never queries Kubernetes on the request path, it keeps everything in memory and pushes updates.

The shared vocabulary lives in the core crate. InboundServer, L106 describes one port as the proxy should see it, ProxyProtocol, L36 enumerates the protocol detected or configured on it — HTTP/1, HTTP/2, gRPC, opaque TLS, or auto-detection with a timeout — and ClientAuthorization, L55 pairs allowed networks with a ClientAuthentication, L64 requirement that ranges from unauthenticated to mesh-TLS-verified identities.

The gRPC surface then follows directly. InboundPolicyServer, L29 implements two methods: a unary get_port, L85 and a streaming watch_port, L118 that keeps pushing policy revisions until the server drains. There is a symmetric OutboundPolicyServer, L29 for routing decisions the proxy makes on the way out. The glue between index and servers is thin: InboundDiscover, L23 implements the discover trait with get_inbound_server, L39, cloning the current snapshot out of the shared index. Reading this stack bottom-up, you can trace a ServerAuthorization YAML file all the way from a Kubernetes watch to a protobuf Authz message inside a hundred lines of code.

Destination: Addresses on the Wire, Profiles on the Rails

The destination service is the proxy’s phone book, and it is the Go heart of the control plane. Main, L28 boots it on port 8086 with a wall of flags for trust domain, cluster domain, and opaque ports. The server built by NewServer, L87 implements two streaming APIs. Get, L148 answers “where can I reach this destination” by subscribing to endpoint updates, and GetProfile, L313 answers “how should I treat requests to it” by streaming service profiles that carry per-route retry and timeout configuration.

The address side is worth a look because it is where Kubernetes vocabulary turns into mesh vocabulary. NewEndpointsWatcher, L83 watches Endpoints and EndpointSlices and publishes address sets per service. Downstream, endpointTranslator, L35 converts those sets into the Destination.Get protobuf stream the proxy consumes, and newEndpointTranslator, L76 captures per-pod details like topology zone so the proxy can prefer same-zone endpoints. For an inference stack, this is the machinery that lets you scale the decode workers behind one Service and have every meshed client re-resolve without restarting anything.

Identity: mTLS Without Ceremony

Every meshed workload gets a certificate naming it in a trust domain, and the issuance path is compact. The identity controller starts from Main, L32 and serves the Certify gRPC API implemented by Certify, L212. That method’s first job is validation: the K8sTokenValidator, L26 turns the workload’s service-account bearer token into a Kubernetes TokenReview, and its Validate, L51 method maps the authenticated username — the system:serviceaccount:namespace:name form — into a Linkerd identity. Only then does the service sign a certificate bound to that identity.

The client side is charmingly explicit: the proxy-identity init container runs before the proxy starts and blocks until it holds a cert. In practice this is why Linkerd’s “zero-config mTLS” claim holds up: nothing in your deployment YAML changes, because the injector already added the init container and the volume mounts that make the handshake possible.

From Install to Your First Model

Enough reading; here is the shortest path from nothing to a meshed inference service, with each step tied to the code that implements it.

First, install the control plane. The CLI entry point newCmdInstall, L89 loads the linkerd-control-plane and linkerd-crds charts (install.go, L38) and renders them with the embedded Helm engine, so the canonical invocation is simply:

linkerd install --crds | kubectl apply -f -
linkerd install    | kubectl apply -f -
linkerd check

newCmdCheck, L92 runs the health checks that verify control-plane pods, webhooks, and API availability before you proceed.

Second, mesh the workloads. You have two ways to add the sidecar. Client-side, NewCmdInject, L50 pipes a manifest through runInjectCmd, L46, and the patch is built by the same ResourceConfig, L629 machinery the webhook uses. Automatic sidecar injection goes through the admission webhook whose Inject, L31 handler is invoked by the Kubernetes API server on pod creation. For a model server, annotate the namespace once and deploy:

kubectl create ns infer && kubectl annotate ns infer linkerd.io/inject=enabled
kubectl apply -f vllm-deploy.yaml -n infer

Third, lock the door. By default, Linkerd’s policy is deny-with-allow-lists once you define a Server for the port. Create a Server selecting your vLLM port, then a ServerAuthorization permitting only your gateway’s identity. The Rust index (saz updates, L25) picks the change up, watch_port streams the new authorizations to the sidecar, and within a watch tick only meshed, authenticated clients get through. The policy kinds are real Kubernetes CRDs in the policy.linkerd.io group, as the protobuf labels (inbound.rs, L238) confirm. A similar gate in front of a metrics sidecar is exactly how you would expose a Prometheus scrape port to the mesh safely.

Honest Limits

A few things this repo tour cannot give you. Most importantly: the data-plane proxy is not here. The README’s repo list is explicit that linkerd2-proxy, L26 — “Linkerd 2.x data plane proxy” — and the gRPC API bindings at linkerd2-proxy-api are separate repositories. What this repo contains is everything around the proxy: the policy decisions it enforces, the addresses it discovers, the certificates it holds, and the containers that install it. If you want to read the Rust HTTP/2 implementation or the byte-level latency tricks, you must go one repository further.

Second, scope: this tour covers the four directories that dominate the control-plane story (cli/, controller/, pkg/, policy-controller/), not the viz/metrics extensions, the multicluster link controller, or the Helm charts in full. Third, no performance numbers here: Linkerd’s latency claims live in its official documentation and benchmarks, and I have not reproduced them — the only thing I claim from source is what each symbol does. Finally, all line numbers point at main as of 2026-11-02; Rust workspaces reorganize often, so treat the links as a snapshot and grep if a symbol has moved. What survives the drift is the architecture: a small Go control plane, a strict Rust policy brain, and a proxy that needs surprisingly little from both to make a model-serving cluster secure by default.
entry.summary: A source tour of Linkerd's Go control plane, Rust policy controller, and the seams that keep it the lightest mesh for Kubernetes.

entry.title: Traefik in the Source: How a Go Reverse Proxy Learns Your Fleet and Rewires Itself Live

link.title: Traefik in the Source: How a Go Reverse Proxy Learns Your Fleet and Rewires Itself Live

entry.content:
If you run more than one model server — a vLLM box here, a FastAPI inference container there, a GPU node pool over in Kubernetes — then the most performance-critical piece of software you own is not the model server. It is the thing that decides, in microseconds, which of those servers should receive the next request. That decision is made at the edge, by a reverse proxy, and when the edge is wrong everything behind it looks slow. Token streams stall while requests sit in the wrong queue. Canaries never get tested under real load. Rolling out a new model version becomes a maintenance window instead of a config edit.

Traefik approaches this problem from an unusual angle. Instead of asking you to describe every route up front, it watches your infrastructure — Docker engines, Kubernetes APIs, plain files — and builds the routing table itself, then keeps rebuilding it as your fleet changes. Need to route api.example.com/v1/embeddings to an embedding fleet and /v1/chat to a chat fleet? With the right provider wired in, you declare that intent where your services already live (labels, CRDs, files) and Traefik translates it into live listeners with zero restarts. For AI/ML workloads this matters more than it sounds: inference fleets scale horizontally, GPU nodes come and go, and you want the routing layer to track reality automatically while you still control weights for canary rollouts of a new checkpoint.

This post is a source-level tour of how Traefik actually does that, read directly from the Go code on the master branch. The two diagrams below were generated from the repository structure: first an overview of the major subsystems, then a deeper pass over the same architecture with the bootstrap, config and routing internals included. Every symbol linked in the text points at a real function in the repository, so you can follow along line by line.

Traefik's main subsystems: the bootstrap wires providers, a configuration watcher, entrypoints and router factories; requests flow from entrypoints through the muxer into load-balanced services; the API exposes runtime state for the dashboard.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Bootstrap. main, L54 parses static configuration and calls setupServer, L180, the single function that assembles every manager, factory and entrypoint you see in the diagram.
  • Providers. NewProviderAggregator, L181 builds the aggregator whose Provide, L178 launches all configured providers against one shared channel — Docker, Kubernetes, files and friends all pushing configuration messages into the same stream.
  • The watcher. NewConfigurationWatcher, L324 creates the core hot-reload loop: receiveConfigurations, L98 deduplicates provider updates and applyConfigurations, L166 merges and broadcasts them.
  • Entrypoints. NewTCPEntryPoint, L184 builds each listener — a keep-alive TCP socket from buildListener, L512 plus one or two Go HTTP servers from newHTTPServer, L643.
  • Routers. CreateRouters, L101 builds HTTP, TCP and UDP routers per entrypoint; the HTTP side goes through NewManager, L55 which validates the router tree in ParseRouterTree, L91.
  • Rules. NewParser, L31 is a predicate parser that turns strings like Host(api.example.com) && PathPrefix(/v1) into matcher trees consumed by the Muxer.AddRoute, L92 call chain.
  • Services. BuildHTTP, L96 resolves a service name into a handler, typically a load balancer built by getLoadBalancerServiceHandler, L435 which proxies to your backends via ProxyBuilder.Build, L41.
  • The API. createRouter, L94 mounts /api/rawdata, /api/overview and the router/service endpoints that power the dashboard at :8080.

The detailed view: static and dynamic configuration types, the merge and model-apply step, per-provider wiring, the HTTP and TCP routing internals, and the observability layer that feeds access logs and metrics.

The Bootstrap Spine: From Binary to First Route

Traefik has one moving picture worth internalizing: configuration flows one way, requests flow the other. Configuration enters at the bottom through providers, gets merged in the middle, and radiates outward to listeners; requests enter at the top through entrypoints and fall down through matchers to services.

In the bootstrap, setupServer, L180 does eight things in order: build the provider aggregator, create the TLS manager, register metric clients and the access log, construct TCP and UDP entrypoints, build the service manager factory, build the router factory, create the configuration watcher, and finally hand everything to NewServer, L403. The Server, L17 type is tiny on purpose — its Start, L47 method just starts the entrypoints and the watcher and then waits on a signal channel. All the intelligence lives in the two halves it connects.

The watcher is the part that makes Traefik feel alive. receiveConfigurations, L98 keeps a map of the latest config per provider, deep-copies and transforms it, and pushes it downstream only when something actually changed; applyConfigurations, L166 then merges everything with mergeConfiguration, L18 and applies the routing model in applyModel, L323. Registered listeners fire after that: TLS configs go to the Manager.UpdateConfigs, L93 method, metrics counters tick, and the switch listener rebuilds routers and swaps them into the live entrypoints via SwitchRouter, L383. A new route exists on the wire without a single connection being dropped.

How Providers Keep the Table Fresh

Every provider implements the same small interface — Provide(channel, pool) — which is why they compose cleanly. The aggregator’s launchProvider, L205 runs each one with optional throttling, so a chatty provider cannot starve the rest.

The file provider is the simplest mental model: Provide, L55 decodes YAML or TOML into a dynamic configuration and, when watching is enabled, addWatcher, L169 attaches fsnotify watchers so an edit is a reload. The Docker provider does the same trick over the Docker API: Provide, L53 lists containers and turns labels into routers and services. The Kubernetes provider is the heavyweight: Provide, L98 watches IngressRoutes and related CRDs, and loadConfigurationFromCRD, L248 converts those objects into Traefik’s own config vocabulary. If you are coming from a Kubernetes background, our Kubernetes primer covers how pods, services and ingress controllers fit together; Traefik simply participates in that world as the controller that consumes the custom resources.

One provider deserves a special mention even though it ships no services: the internal one, named "internal" at ProviderName, L22. It contributes the api@internal and dashboard services that the API handler serves, and it is the provider the watcher waits for before applying the first configuration.

How a Request Flows Through the Routing Core

A request hits an entrypoint socket, is accepted by the loop in Start, L255, and is handed to the current TCP router through a handler switcher. The TCP router at ServeTCP, L101 peeks at the first bytes to decide TLS or plain TCP, routes on SNI where applicable, and for HTTP traffic forwards the connection into a Go HTTP server where the real matching begins.

That matching is the muxer: ServeHTTP, L48 walks registered routes and dispatches to the first matcher tree that returns true. Router priority, provider precedence and negated matchers all resolve here. Before the match even happens, the request has already passed through the entrypoint chain built by newHTTPServer, L643 — forwarded-header handling, path normalization and keep-alive limits.

Once a router matches, the middleware chain built by BuildMiddlewareChain, L69 wraps the service handler: rate limiting, circuit breaking, retries, header manipulation, or your own chain of middlewares. Observability wraps everything: the observability manager defined at ObservabilityMgr, L23 wires metrics and tracing, and the access log handler’s ServeHTTP, L190 captures request and response fields for every round trip, logged after the response completes in logTheRoundTrip, L355. For inference traffic, that access log line — with the router name, service name and duration — is often the cheapest per-request telemetry you can get, and it exports cleanly to a Prometheus setup alongside Traefik’s own metrics endpoints, ready for dashboards once you wire in Grafana.

Finally the service layer. BuildHTTP, L96 rejects multi-type services, checks for recursion, and builds the handler: weighted round robin at getWRRServiceHandler, L323, mirroring at getMirrorServiceHandler, L286, failover, or a plain proxy. The resulting proxy, built through NewProxyBuilder, L29, is where your request finally leaves Traefik for a backend — with connection pooling, transport settings and TLS handled by the transport manager configured from serversTransports.

From Install to Your First Model

The fastest path is a single container run straight from the README:

docker run -d -p 8080:8080 -p 80:80 -v $PWD/traefik.toml:/etc/traefik/traefik.toml traefik

That maps the dashboard port 8080 and the HTTP port 80, and mounts one TOML file. The minimal static side of that file matches the repository’s own sample:

[entryPoints]
  [entryPoints.web]
    address = ":80"

[api]
  dashboard = true

Static configuration — entrypoints, providers, the API — is read once at startup and describes what Traefik listens on. Everything dynamic lives with the providers. The two-level split is enforced in the type system: static.Configuration at Configuration, L86 with its EntryPoints map at L90, versus dynamic.Configuration at Configuration, L23 holding routers, services, middlewares and TLS.

Now point it at something real. Suppose your inference backend is a FastAPI service exposing /v1/embeddings; our FastAPI walkthrough shows how to build one. Add a dynamic file next to the static one:

[http]
  [http.routers.to-model-api]
    rule = "Host(`api.example.com`) && PathPrefix(`/v1`)"
    service = "model-api"

  [http.services.model-api.loadBalancer]
    [[http.services.model-api.loadBalancer.servers]]
      url = "http://10.0.0.11:8000"
    [[http.services.model-api.loadBalancer.servers]]
      url = "http://10.0.0.12:8000"

Save it, and the file provider’s fsnotify watcher fires, the watcher merges and broadcasts, the router factory rebuilds, and SwitchRouter puts the new route live — no restart, no dropped connections. Two servers in the load balancer means you already have failover; to canary a new model version, add a third server with a low weight, watch the access logs and metrics, then shift the weight as confidence grows. On Kubernetes, the same result comes from an IngressRoute CRD instead of a TOML block, watched continuously by the CRD provider — and remember that token streaming backends need generous read timeouts so long generations are not cut mid-stream.

Honest Limits

  • Configuration plumbing is YAML/TOML/labels, not code. Routing rules are expressive but stringly typed; complex header surgery or request rewriting logic belongs in your application or a dedicated middleware, not in ever-longer rule expressions.
  • No built-in token-aware routing. Traefik balances requests, not tokens or model latency. If you want routing decisions based on prompt size or per-token cost, you build that in the application tier behind the proxy.
  • Watch the timeout defaults for LLM traffic. Long streaming responses are fine over HTTP, but aggressive responding timeouts on an entrypoint will truncate slow generations; set read and write timeouts deliberately for inference entrypoints.
  • The dashboard is a window, not a control plane. It exposes runtime state read-only (plus ACME user actions); fleet changes still flow through your providers — GitOps, Kubernetes CRDs or files.
  • Deep Kubernetes integration means CRDs. Native Kubernetes Ingress support is limited compared to the CRD provider; to use Traefik fully in a cluster you adopt its custom resource definitions, which is a real ecosystem commitment.

Where does Traefik sit in the stack? Above the service mesh and below your application frameworks: it terminates TLS at the edge, keeps a live map of your fleet, and routes with enough middleware depth to protect expensive GPU-backed services from accidental overload. Read the bootstrap once with the diagrams open and the whole design — providers feeding a watcher feeding swappable routers — is one of the cleaner pieces of Go infrastructure code you will find.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of Traefik: entrypoints, rule parsing, hot-reload watchers, providers, load balancers and the API behind the dashboard.
